name: Parallax & Apparent Motion
summary: Observer movement and viewing geometry can make a nearby slow object appear to move rapidly against a distant background. Physical motion requires range, timing and platform context.

referenceSources.label: Haqq-Misra and colleagues — Infrared bird hypothesis (v4)

scienceResearch.intro: Observer movement and viewing geometry can make a nearby slow object appear to move rapidly against a distant background. Physical motion requires range, timing and platform context.
scienceResearch.keyPrinciple: Apparent image behavior needs calibrated context before it becomes a physical measurement.
scienceResearch.keyPrincipleSupport: Established imaging principles and paper-specific hypotheses carry different evidentiary weight.

foundation.title: Relative viewpoint
foundation.text: From a moving vehicle, nearby objects appear to shift against distant scenery. The relative displacement depends on geometry and distance; apparent screen motion is not a direct speedometer.

foundation.title: What measurements are needed?
foundation.text: Recovering motion requires known timing, angular scale, range and observer motion. Different combinations can produce similar image tracks.

foundation.title: Applied UAP research
foundation.text: The PURSUE kinematic study illustrates ambiguity in PR113 and a constrained relative-speed estimate in PR149. Its conclusions concern the public recordings analyzed, rather than all UAP evidence.

foundation.title: Birds and PR135
foundation.text: A separate preprint proposes a nearer flock as an explanation for PR135 using brightness measurements and geometry. Missing telemetry leaves this interpretation open to testing.

foundation.title: Limits
foundation.text: Parallax is a geometric effect, not an object identity. Demonstrating a possible geometry does not prove that it occurred in a particular case.
